name: TLV73310PDBVR
title: TLV733P 300 mA capacitor-free low-dropout regulator, fixed 1.0 V to 3.3 V output
summary: The TLV733P is a family of fixed-output PMOS low-dropout regulators for loads up to 300 mA, running from 1.4 V to 5.5 V input with 34 µA typical ground current. Its control loop stays stable with no input or output capacitor at all, and also with ceramic capacitors fitted; leaving the output capacitor off removes start-up inrush. Protection is a foldback current limit, thermal shutdown and input undervoltage lockout, and a 120 Ω switch discharges the output whenever the part is off. TLV73310PDBVR is the 1.0 V version in the 5-pin SOT-23 (DBV) on a 3000-piece reel; a 1 mm × 1 mm 4-pin X2SON (DQN) is the other package.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The regulator alone between a supply and a load: IN takes the supply, OUT feeds the load, GND goes to ground and EN is driven high to switch the output on and low to switch it off. The input and output capacitors are both optional; the part regulates with either, both or neither fitted.

parts.note: input capacitor, may be left off
output capacitor, may be left off

circuits.title: DC-DC converter post regulation
circuits.description: A 1.5 V TLV733P cleans up the 1.8 V output of a switching converter for a load drawing 200 mA continuous and 300 mA peak. 1 µF ceramic capacitors sit on both IN and OUT, which this design needs to keep the output within 10 % on a fast 50 mA to 200 mA load step. EN is the on/off control.
notes: The 1.2 V option's dropout is typically below 300 mV at 125 °C (Figure 7), and the 1.5 V option's is lower. Junction temperature is checked against the maximum-ambient curve (Figure 34).

circuits.title: Capacitor-free operation from a battery
circuits.description: Two 1.5 V cells, 3.0 V falling to 1.8 V, feed a 1.0 V TLV733P with no capacitors at all, for a 100 mA load. EN is tied to IN so the output is on whenever the battery is connected. The cells' low impedance makes an input capacitor unnecessary, and with no output capacitor there is no charging surge at start-up, which keeps input current under its 200 mA limit.

operation.text: The output stays off until VIN passes the rising UVLO threshold (1.3 V typical, 1.4 V maximum) and turns off again when VIN drops below the falling threshold (1.25 V typical). While locked out, OUT is pulled to ground through 120 Ω.

EN is active high: above VEN(HI) (0.9 V min) the part regulates, below VEN(LO) (0.35 V max) it shuts down. EN has no pull-down of its own; where no on/off control is wanted, EN is connected to IN. When disabled, a MOSFET switches a 120 Ω resistor from OUT to ground; the output then decays with the time constant of COUT against the 120 Ω in parallel with the load.

The allowed current falls as the output voltage falls. Into a short the output supplies about 150 mA (1.0 V version) to 170 mA (3.3 V version). In limit the output is unregulated and equals the limited current times the load resistance. A sustained short heats the pass device until thermal shutdown, and the part then cycles between current limit and shutdown for as long as the fault lasts. During start-up the foldback holds current below the nominal-voltage limit ILIM (Figures 18 to 20), so a constant-current load, or an output pulled negative at enable, can stop the output from rising fully; such loads are kept off until the output has reached its nominal value.
The PMOS pass element has a body diode from OUT to IN. If OUT is held above IN this diode conducts and large current can flow, so the output must not be forced above the input.

The output turns off at about 160 °C junction temperature and back on at about 140 °C, so under heavy dissipation the part may cycle. Junction temperature is to be kept at or below 125 °C in normal use; running repeatedly into thermal shutdown reduces reliability. Margin can be checked by raising ambient temperature under worst-case load until protection trips.

Normal regulation needs VIN above both the UVLO threshold and VOUT(nom) + VDO, EN above VEN(HI), load below the current limit and junction below the shutdown temperature. With VIN between the UVLO threshold and VOUT(nom) + VDO the part is in dropout: the pass device is fully on and VOUT equals VIN minus the dropout voltage; line or load transients in this mode can produce large output deviations. Any one of low VIN, low EN or over-temperature disables the part, and the pull-down then discharges the output.

Neither capacitor is required for stability. An output capacitor of 0.1 µF or more improves dynamic response; X5R and X7R ceramics are named for their stable value and ESR over temperature. 0.1 µF to 1 µF from IN to GND helps with reactive sources, transients, input ripple and PSRR, and an input capacitor is called for when the source impedance exceeds 0.5 Ω, with a larger value for fast heavy load steps or a supply several inches away. Below about 0.1 A/µs load slew the response is much the same with or without an output capacitor; above it the deviation grows quickly without one (Figure 33), so loads with faster edges get an output capacitor. The maximum recommended output capacitance is 100 µF. Leaving out the output capacitor saves space and cost and lowers start-up inrush, at the price of larger output deviations.

In dropout the PMOS pass device is in its linear region and behaves as its on-resistance, so dropout voltage grows roughly in proportion to load current. As the input-output difference shrinks toward dropout, ripple rejection and transient response get worse. Lower output-voltage versions have higher dropout (Figures 7 to 12).

Heat leaves through the board copper around the part; heavier copper and plated through-holes into heat-spreading layers improve it. Figure 34 gives the maximum ambient temperature against dissipation for both packages on a JEDEC high-K board in still air, keeping the junction at or below 125 °C.

IN is fed from a supply with low output impedance. Inductance between the supply and IN can cause large voltage swings at IN during start-up and load steps; where it cannot be avoided an input capacitor is used.

Input and output capacitors go as close to the part as possible. Device connections use copper planes, with thermal vias around the part to spread heat. On the DQN package no via is placed directly under the thermal pad, since it can draw solder away from the pad joint during reflow. Vias under paste, if used, are filled, plugged or tented.
The TLV73312PEVM-643 evaluation module carries the 1.2 V version.
An AEC-Q100 qualified version is offered as TLV733P-Q1.
